notable_claims: Network administrators may block entire sites to avoid managing individual user behavior.
The NSFNET AUP contains an escape clause allowing the NSF Project Office to determine what uses are consistent with network purposes.
The author claims that, at the time of writing, no such official determinations by the NSF had been reported to the community; actions were taken voluntarily by sites.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the tension between academic freedom and network administration policies concerning offensive or erotic material. The author argues that while information providers may not be legally required to censor content, network administrators have the right to sever links to sites that violate their local policies. The post also discusses the NSFNET Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) and the potential for the NSF to determine what constitutes a 'consistent use' of the network.
classification.title: Re: The USENET pornographic network

notable_claims: The court in Cubby, Inc. v. CompuServe ruled that online services are more like bookstores/distributors than publishers.
Liability for defamation on such platforms requires 'actual knowledge' of the content.
Holding service providers liable for all user content would create a burden that conflicts with First Amendment protections.
classification.summary: Mike Godwin discusses the legal implications of Cubby, Inc. v. CompuServe, where a court held that an online service provider is not liable for defamatory content unless it has 'actual knowledge' of it. The decision compared CompuServe to a bookstore or library rather than a publisher, arguing that requiring pre-screening of all user posts would chill First Amendment rights. This case served as an early legal precedent regarding the liability of system operators and online service providers.
classification.title: Effect of the Compuserve decision

identity.subject: Re: Effect of the Compuserve decision

notable_claims: Questioning if examining and deciding to keep content makes a BBS operator liable for that content.
Concern that the need to avoid 'risky' material creates a chilling effect on electronic forums.
classification.summary: Brad Templeton discusses the legal implications of liability for online service providers and BBS operators regarding obscene or defamatory content. He draws parallels between electronic forums and physical bookstores or record stores, questioning whether monitoring content creates a 'chilling effect' or increases legal liability. The post reflects early concerns over the role of online editors and the application of existing obscenity laws to digital spaces.
classification.title: Effect of the Compuserve decision

identity.subject: Re: Effect of the Compuserve decision

notable_claims: CompuServe won a summary judgment dismissal in the CI$ case.
Lack of pre-screening is a key factor in determining if a forum operator is treated as a 'bookstore' rather than a 'publisher'.
Post-hoc removal of content does not automatically make a service provider liable as a publisher.
classification.summary: Mike Godwin of the EFF discusses a legal decision regarding CompuServe and the liability of online forum operators for defamatory content. He distinguishes between moderators who pre-screen messages (acting like publishers) and those who do not (acting like bookstores). The discussion emphasizes that post-hoc removal of material does not necessarily transform a service provider into a publisher.
classification.title: Re: The CI$ Case

notable_claims: Some state laws exempt libraries from minor-access restrictions.
A judge in the CompuServe decision characterized CIS as an electronic, for-profit library.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the potential for online services like BBSs and Usenet sites to be legally classified as libraries to gain exemptions from minor-access laws. He cites American Library Association policy against age-based access restrictions and references a court decision describing CompuServe's CIS as an electronic library.
classification.title: Re: [URGENT]: ACCESS LAWS TO SEXUALLY-EXPLICIT ONLINE MATERIAL

identity.subject: Re: [URGENT]: ACCESS LAWS TO SEXUALLY-EXPLICIT ONLINE MATERIAL

notable_claims: Over 20 University of Wyoming users were 'dis-usered' for using IRC.
Reinstatement of accounts required a formal agreement to refrain from IRC-related activities.
University consultants described IRC as being like a 'disease' in terms of its spread among users.
classification.summary: Robert Wedlock reports that the University of Wyoming banned Internet Relay Chat (IRC) on its VAX cluster and Ultrix systems. Over 20 users had their accounts disabled, with reinstatement conditioned upon removing IRC files and agreeing to refrain from IRC activities. The administration characterized IRC as a 'disease' that spread rapidly across user directories.
classification.title: IRC outlawed at U Wyoming

notable_claims: Public universities are constrained by the U.S. Constitution and state constitutions regarding searches and due process.
Suspending computer users before establishing wrongdoing is morally wrong.
Searching user computer files without authorization similar to that required for a professor's office is morally wrong.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a debate regarding the University of Wyoming's ban on IRC and its handling of user accounts. He argues that public universities are constrained by constitutional law, student codes, and moral obligations toward academic freedom. Specifically, he criticizes the university for suspending users without due process and searching computer files without proper authorization.
classification.title: IRC outlawed at U Wyoming...

notable_claims: State universities may not be as 'whimsical' as private organizations in revoking computer accounts due to legal or contractual requirements for due process.
classification.summary: Christopher Davis of the EFF responds to a debate regarding the banning of Internet Relay Chat (IRC) at the University of Wyoming. He argues that because state universities are government agencies, they may be subject to due process and contractual obligations when revoking computer access, unlike private entities.
classification.title: Re: IRC outlawed at U Wyoming...

identity.subject: Re: IRC outlawed at U Wyoming...

notable_claims: A court order required U.C. Berkeley to search all computers for files containing a specific student's login name.
The Buckley Amendment may take precedence over the Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986 (ECPA) in certain educational contexts.
S.266 was viewed as an attempt by Congress to require back doors for encryption.
Wide 'fishing expedition' searches are used by litigation firms to prove damages in civil cases.
classification.summary: A summary of a KQED Forum discussion regarding the distinctions between hackers and crackers, corporate privacy policies, and government surveillance. The post highlights a legal case at U.C. Berkeley involving court-ordered wide searches of computers for student files. It also discusses legislative efforts like S.266 and the tension between law enforcement search warrants and digital privacy.
classification.title: hackers, crackers, privacy on KQED

notable_claims: A court order required UC Berkeley to search all files on mainframes Garnet and Violet for a specific student's login name.
The university argued that printing and manually reviewing 11 million lines of search results constituted an undue burden.
The Buckley amendment to the California Family Education Rights and Privacy Act was used to justify the search of university-maintained computer systems.
classification.summary: A student's family sued UC Berkeley, leading to a court order requiring the university to search two mainframes for any files containing the student's login ID or name. The case highlights a conflict between a student's right to access their records under the Buckley amendment and the privacy of other users whose files were swept up in bulk searches. University lawyers contested the order based on undue burden rather than privacy violations.
classification.title: UC computer searches

identity.subject: UC computer searches (was Re: hackers, crackers, privacy on KQED)

notable_claims: Public institutions like state universities may find it illegal to enforce gender-based restrictions on forums.
Enforcement of charters is not possible for groups in the ALT hierarchy.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the feasibility and legality of enforcing gender-based restrictions on Usenet newsgroups. The author argues that enforcement is impossible for groups created in the 'alt' hierarchy.
classification.title: Re: ALT.womyn.ONLY
